title: A U.S.-Market Kei Truck … with a Scion Badge? It’s Happening

body_markdown:
Adventurous with design, entirely unique, and eye-catching in their own weird way” is how we described the vehicles built by Toyota subbrand Scion in our 2025 article[“9 Automotive Brands We Miss.”](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/our-two-cents-9-automotive-brands-we-miss/) We won’t need to miss it much longer, because in the second half of 2027, Scion will return, under the label “Scion by Toyota,” with a kei truck assembled and sold in the United States.


There is a lot to unpack. No, kei trucks[aren’t suddenly legal in all 50 states](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/the-kei-kerfuffle-states-struggle-over-what-to-do-with-these-tiny-trucklets/) . The KEI-01 isn’t—for now—your regular mass-production, available-to-the-public vehicle. As a “low-speed vehicle” under the[Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 500](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.500) , it will be limited to speeds below 25 mph. That said, the right-hand-drive trucklet will be built in Indiana alongside popular Toyota people-haulers like the Highlander, Grand Highlander, and Sienna minivan. At launch, Toyota intends to sell the KEI-01 in “intentionally” low volumes. The kei truck will initially only be available to fleet customers through “a small network” of existing Toyota dealers.


Whoever chose the black-and-yellow Costco storage tote for this shoot, bravo.


Toyota


Toyota has anticipated an enthusiast’s natural next question: When can the general public buy one of these? “Based on market conditions, customer demand, and operational considerations, Toyota may consider expanding availability to limited retail sales at a later date.”


Toyota may have already cracked the door, because the list of customers whose needs would be met by a KEI-01 lists “outdoor enthusiasts and hobbyists” after small business owners, farmers, universities, and delivery providers. That said, don’t take what we read between the lines of Toyota’s press release as a clear-cut promise. For example, how would one prove you are an outdoor enthusiast? A quarter of the U.S. casually wears camouflage, for goodness’ sake! ( *Statistic not scientifically verified.* — *Ed.* )


Toyota


Compared to the older models imported under the 25-year import rule, this is one bougie kei truck. Air conditioning comes standard in the extended-length cab, as does heat and a continuously variable transmission. The seats both recline and slide. The 4WD system is “selectable,” suggesting that the 660cc three-cylinder engine and CVT send power to the front or rear pair of wheels by default (thus saving on fuel). When we asked Toyota to tell us more about the system, including which were the primary drive wheels, and what “auto mode” and “push-button lock-up” are, it declined to share more information, so we’re left with educated guesses. Best we can tell, the decision to use 2WD vs. 4WD is up to the vehicle’s computer brain, and locking the differential (differentials?) is up to the driver. Makes sense, because the people to whom Toyota is initially marketing this vehicle—farmers, ranchers, universities, delivery providers—care about saving money on fuel economy and about tackling off-road terrain.


Toyota


Payload is slightly lower than the traditional 350-kg (~772-pound) standard of older Japanese-market vehicles, at 600 pounds, but like those vehicles, the KEI-01 will be able to tow. Toyota doesn’t provide a tow rating, stopping at “small trailers and equipment.” Nose to tail, the KEI-01 measures less than 11 feet, and it’s under 5 feet wide. The sides of the bed are hinged at the bottom, so that you can access the bed from either side or the back of the truck.


What else can we expect from the Scion brand? Experimentation, according to Toyota. It has a broad range of vehicles in mind, as indicated by the SxS Concept (a Scion-branded[side-by-side](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/toyota-might-revive-the-scion-brand-as-a-side-by-side/) we covered last year, when it debuted at the[Specialty Equipment Market Association](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/sema/) show) and the BKE Concept, which we’re pretty sure is the little bike on the back of the KEI-01 below. These three vehicles are a great place to start, considering that the main reason we loved the Scion brand was funkiness. Whatever you do, Toyota, keep the new Scion weird!


Toyota
